The same team presented "lighter logging for 300 ms faster responses" with its reversal cost, rebuilding the audit trail for a regulated workflow, and the sponsor rejected it. When a question asks what is missing from a trade-off presentation, the answer is often the cost of changing course later. Options that explain the trade-off in implementation detail to a CFO or business sponsor are weaker than ones that state the business consequence.

The right revision states the trade-off, the rejected alternatives and the residual risk with its evidence, and meets the constraint directly. Reject revisions that claim certainty about model behaviour, drop the alternatives, or answer a different stakeholder's concern.

Operational Handoff Completeness. Check a Claude system's handoff package for the missing assumption, dependency or runbook that would block the team taking it over, and write the documentation that closes the gap.

The architect who designed a system will not run it forever. A successor who inherits diagrams and code but not the reasons will, sooner or later, "simplify" something that was there for a reason: switch to a global endpoint, remove an approval step, drop a log field. Documentation exists to prevent that, and to let auditors check that controls are real.

docs.c: Could a competent stranger change it safely?
docs.x: If an architect who was not involved could read the documentation and make a change without breaking a requirement, it is complete. If they would have to guess why something is the way it is, it is not.

docs.h: Decision logs travel with the system
docs.x: The package includes the decision log (lesson 6.2), with each decision's rationale and the alternatives that were rejected. Without them, a successor cannot tell a deliberate control from an accident, and removes the one that looked redundant.

For the person taking over For the compliance reviewer Explains intent Architecture diagram, decision log, assumption register Control register (obligation, control, owner) Shows evidence Deployment runbook, test and evaluation results Control register with links to evidence Artifact Records Assumption register What is not yet confirmed, and who will confirm it Decision log What was chosen, what was rejected, and why Architecture diagram Components, data flows, trust boundaries Runbook How to deploy, operate, roll back and respond to incidents Evaluation summary What was tested, on what data, with what results Control register Obligations mapped to controls, owners and evidence

Handoffs also go forward , to the team that builds. Give them the requirements with sources, the decisions with rationale, the success criteria and evaluation set, interface contracts (tool definitions, schemas), the prompt templates and their versioning rules, and the non-negotiables ("medication lists are inserted by code, never generated"). For AI systems, prompts, model versions and evaluation sets are part of the design and need the same care as code.

A handoff package is complete when the team that will run the system can operate it, change it and recover it without calling the architect. Check it against three lists. Element Includes What breaks without it Assumptions Volumes, input sizes, languages, peak times, each with its source The team cannot tell when traffic has moved outside what the design supports Dependencies Model version and its retirement date, deployment surface and region, MCP servers and their owners, rate limits and quotas, secrets and who rotates them A deprecation, quota or expired credential takes the system down with no one prepared Runbooks Alert-to-action steps: rate-limit storm, provider outage and fallback, quality drop, suspected injection, model migration The on-call engineer improvises during an incident Evaluation suite The dataset, how to run it, the thresholds that gate a release Nobody can tell whether a prompt or model change is safe Owners Who owns each component, and the escalation path Problems wait for someone to decide whose they are

Models are versioned and eventually retired. Pin versions in production, track deprecation notices, and keep the evaluation suite ready so a migration is a planned release, not an emergency. The regression suite is what makes this routine.

docs.t: Packaging and Distributing Claude Code Workflows
docs.x: A workflow that works well for one team (a review Skill, a couple of hooks, a subagent, some slash commands, an MCP server) rarely survives being copied by hand to forty others. Copies drift, nobody can update them, and the safety controls that made it trustworthy get dropped. Scaling it is an architecture decision with four parts: packaging, distribution, central versus team controls, and rollout.

docs.t: Packaging and Distributing Claude Code Workflows
docs.x: A plugin bundles the pieces of a workflow into one versioned unit: Skills, slash commands, subagent definitions, hooks and MCP server configuration. Teams install the plugin, not the parts, and an update reaches everyone who has it. Plugins are published in a marketplace , a catalogue that Claude Code reads from a git repository, a URL or a local path. An organization usually runs its own marketplace beside Anthropic's official one. Control (managed settings) What it does extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins Register the organization's marketplace on every machine and require named plugins strictKnownMarketplaces Allow plugins only from the listed marketplace sources blockedMarketplaces Block named sources outright disableSideloadFlags Stop users loading plugins from a local folder or URL on the command line enabledPlugins set to false Block one plugin everywhere, even from an allowed marketplace Managed settings reach every machine through the admin console, device management or a managed settings file, and users cannot override them. Runs in CI or containers can load plugins from a pre-built seed directory instead of cloning a marketplace at runtime.

docs.t: Packaging and Distributing Claude Code Workflows
docs.c: Put musts in settings, shoulds in instructions
docs.x: Claude Code reads configuration at several levels, and the difference between them matters. Layer What it does Use for Organization-managed settings Set by administrators; override user and project settings Rules that must hold everywhere: denied commands and paths, allowed tools, approved model choices Project settings (in the repository) Shared by everyone working in that project Project permissions, hooks, MCP servers the project needs Instruction files (CLAUDE.md) at organization, project and user level Load standing context and conventions into every session Coding standards, repository layout, how to run tests User settings Personal preferences Editor habits, personal shortcuts Instruction files are guidance : Claude follows them, but they cannot prevent an action. Permissions, managed settings and hooks are enforcement . Anything that must never happen ("never read .env files", "never push to main") belongs in permission rules or hooks, not only in an instruction file. If breaking a rule would be an incident, enforce it with managed settings, permissions or a hook. Instruction files are for conventions and context.

docs.t: Packaging and Distributing Claude Code Workflows
docs.x: Decide for each control who owns it. Enforce centrally what must hold everywhere, especially when a workflow runs unattended in CI or on a schedule, where nobody is watching to catch a mistake: denied paths and commands, which marketplaces are allowed, whether risky permission modes can be used, and the hooks that guard secrets and protected branches. Leave to teams what varies by codebase: their own conventions, test commands and project Skills. A control left to each team is a control some team will forget.

A shared asset with no way to roll back can push one bad change to every engineer at once.

docs.c: A rule that was only a suggestion · Security rules in an instruction file only · Big-bang rollout
docs.x: 1. Pilot with a champion in each team , who adapts the shared setup, finds the useful workflows and writes them down. 2. Expand in batches , team by team, with the champion supporting each batch. 3. Measure and adjust : usage, outcomes (cycle time, review findings), costs and feedback, before the next batch. Two failure patterns to avoid: lumpy adoption (a few heavy users, everyone else idle, so practice never standardizes) and stalling at chat (teams use it to ask questions but never adopt repository-aware workflows, Skills or tool integrations, because nobody enabled them). A team's CLAUDE.md said "never modify files under /migrations". After an engineer approved a batch of edits without reading them, a migration file changed. The rule moved into a deny permission in the project settings, plus a hook that blocks any edit to that path, and the instruction file now explains why. Options that rely on CLAUDE.md to stop secret access, destructive commands or protected-branch pushes are weaker than ones that use permissions, managed settings or hooks. "Give everyone access on Monday" is usually wrong in a scenario about adoption. Champions and batches turn access into consistent practice.

Distractors copy folders between teams, put enforcement in instruction files, or let every team fork the workflow.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.x: Agent SDK and Claude Code Configuration. Configure Claude Code and the Agent SDK for a team workflow (permission modes, deny rules, hooks, subagent definitions and headless or CI runs) so it stays inside its safety guardrails, including when nobody is watching.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.x: Claude Code and the Agent SDK share one model of control: permission modes decide how much runs without asking, rules allow or deny specific tools and paths, hooks run your own code at points in the loop, and subagents get their own instructions and tools. This skill asks you to combine them so a team workflow runs as freely as it safely can.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.c: Unattended means pre-approved or denied
docs.x: Mode Behaviour Fits default (Manual) Reads run; edits, commands and network access ask first Sensitive work, unfamiliar code acceptEdits File edits in the working directory run without asking; other actions keep their rules Working with changes reviewed afterwards in the diff plan Claude explores and writes a plan; source edits wait until the plan is approved Understanding a codebase before changing it auto A classifier reviews actions before they run and blocks those that look risky or driven by hostile content Long interactive tasks with fewer prompts; reduces prompts, does not guarantee safety dontAsk Anything not pre-approved by a rule is denied; the session never waits for input Locked-down CI and scripts bypassPermissions Permission prompts and safety checks are skipped Isolated containers or VMs only Two facts matter in many items. Deny rules block in every mode , including bypassPermissions , so they are the hard limit. And administrators can disable bypassPermissions and auto through managed settings , which users and projects cannot override. A run nobody watches must never wait for an approval. Use dontAsk with explicit allow rules for what it may do, deny rules for what it must never do, and hooks for checks that need code.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.x: Hooks run your code at points such as before a tool call ( PreToolUse ), after it ( PostToolUse ) or when a session ends. A PreToolUse hook can inspect the command or file path and block it, which makes a rule like "never push to main " deterministic. Hooks also run formatters and linters after edits, and record what the agent did for audit.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.x: A subagent is defined with its own prompt and its own restricted tool list . A review subagent that only reads files cannot change them, whatever it is asked. Defining subagents per role keeps the main session's context lean and limits what each part of a workflow can do.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.c: A run that stalled for six hours · bypassPermissions to stop stalls · Safety rules only in CLAUDE.md
docs.x: Claude Code runs non-interactively with -p , returning structured output that a pipeline can parse. In CI, pair it with dontAsk , an explicit allow list (for example the test command and file edits), deny rules for secrets and protected branches, and hooks for anything that needs checking in code. The Agent SDK offers the same controls in code, including a permission callback that decides each tool request. A nightly job that triaged failing tests ran in default mode. It reached a command that needed approval at 1 a.m. and waited until morning. Switching to dontAsk with allow rules for the test runner and edits, deny rules for secrets/ and pushes to main , and a PreToolUse hook that logs and blocks any push, made the run finish unattended inside its guardrails. It removes the checks the guardrails depend on and offers no protection against injected instructions. The fix for stalls is pre-approval, not removal of control. Instructions guide behaviour but block nothing. A rule that must hold goes in deny rules, managed settings or a hook.

docs.t: Configuring the Agent SDK and Claude Code
docs.x: Configuration items describe a team workflow with safety and automation requirements (interactive or unattended, what must never happen, how much can run without review) and ask which mode, rules, hooks or subagent definitions fit. Use dontAsk with allow and deny rules for CI, plan before large changes, acceptEdits when edits are reviewed afterwards, deny rules and hooks for hard limits, restricted tool lists for subagents, and managed settings to forbid risky modes. Distractors use bypassPermissions outside an isolated environment, rely on instructions, or leave an unattended run waiting for approval.

docs.x: Northgate wants a nightly job that uses Claude Code to migrate one service at a time to the new logging library, run the tests and open a draft pull request. It runs on a CI runner with no one watching. Security requires: no secrets read into context, no pushes to protected branches, no production access, and SOC 2 evidence of what the job did. 1. Choose the permission mode and justify it. 2. Write the allow rules, deny rules and hooks. Done when: every security requirement is enforced by a rule or a hook, not an instruction. 3. Define one subagent the job uses, with its tool list. 4. Say what is set centrally in managed settings and what is set in the repository. 1. Accountability for AI-Generated Code. Keep people accountable for AI-generated code: put assistance where it helps, give Claude ways to verify its work, and keep a review discipline in which a named person understands and answers for what ships.

The value of AI-assisted development comes from improving the workflow a team already has, not from bolting a chat window beside it. The architect's job is to put assistance where it helps and to keep the quality bar where it was.

Stage How Claude helps What still needs a person Understanding Exploring an unfamiliar codebase, explaining code, tracing a flow Judging whether the explanation is right Planning Proposing an approach and the files to change, before any edit Approving the plan Writing Implementations, tests, boilerplate, refactors from a clear specification Correctness, security and design review Reviewing Summarizing a diff, flagging likely issues, checking conventions in CI The decision to merge Debugging Hypotheses from symptoms, logs and traces Confirming the hypothesis against evidence

docs.h: Practices that make the output better
docs.x: - Explore, then plan, then code. Asking Claude to read the relevant code and propose a plan before editing produces better changes than asking for code straight away. A read-only planning mode helps. - Give it a way to check itself. Tests, a build, a linter, a screenshot to compare against: when Claude can run the check, it can find and fix its own mistakes before a person sees them. - Small, reviewable changes. Large AI-generated diffs are hard to review well. Break work into steps a reviewer can actually read. - Parallel sessions for independent work , each in its own working copy (for example git worktrees), so tasks do not interfere. - Automation in CI. Running Claude non-interactively with structured output lets it review pull requests, triage failures or update documentation as pipeline steps, with deterministic checks (hooks, tests) around it.

docs.c: The author must understand what ships
docs.x: AI makes code cheaper to produce, so more of it reaches review. The bar does not move. A team checklist for any AI-assisted change covers: Dimension The change passes when Correctness Tests cover the requirement and its edge cases, and they pass Security No secrets, inputs validated, least-privilege access for any new calls Maintainability It follows team conventions and introduces no unexplained complexity Understanding The author can explain what it does, why, and how it handles inputs no test covered Passing tests is not the same as understanding. The person who submits a change is accountable for it, whoever or whatever wrote it. The risk the last row guards against is judgment erosion : a team that ships code it no longer understands because it looked right and passed shallow checks, until an input nobody reasoned about reaches production.

docs.c: Faster code, slower reviews · "Tests pass, so it can merge" · AI review as the final verdict
docs.x: Track workflow outcomes, not just usage: pull request cycle time, review rework, escaped defects, time spent on toil. A tool that speeds up writing but slows down review, or raises defects, has not improved the workflow. After adopting AI-assisted coding, a team's pull requests doubled in size and review time per pull request rose by 70%; cycle time barely improved. Splitting work into smaller changes, asking for a plan before code, and requiring authors to annotate non-obvious generated sections brought review time back down and cut cycle time by a third. Options that treat green tests as sufficient for AI-generated code skip the understanding and security checks. The better option keeps the full review bar. An automated review is input to a person's decision, not the decision. Options that let an AI reviewer approve merges on its own are usually wrong.

Control Why it works A named human owner for every merged change Someone answers for it after release Branch protection that requires a human approval; automated accounts cannot approve A person stays in the merge decision The author explains the change in their own words Understanding is checked, not assumed Size limits on pull requests Reviews stay meaningful The same review bar for generated and hand-written code Generated code gets no easier path to production

Accountability items describe a team's review and merge process after it adopted AI-assisted development, usually after something went wrong: rubber-stamped approvals, huge pull requests, an author who could not explain a change. Pick the control that keeps a person accountable: the author must understand and defend the change, a human approval is required before merge, changes stay small enough to review, and the review bar is the same for generated code. Distractors let a model approve, treat passing tests as enough, reward volume, or ban the tool instead of governing it.

docs.h: Apply it: Improve Northgate's pull request workflow
docs.x: Northgate's median pull request cycle time is 26 hours. Three months into the pilot, champions report: AI-assisted pull requests are larger, reviewers struggle with them, and two recent incidents came from generated code that "looked fine" and that the author could not later explain. 1. Redesign the workflow from task to merge, showing where Claude helps and where people decide. 2. Write Northgate's verification checklist for AI-assisted changes, with one concrete check per dimension. Done when: the understanding check would have caught the two incidents. 3. Choose three measures to show whether the changes worked. 1. Workflow 1. Engineer asks Claude to explore the relevant code and propose a plan (read-only planning). Engineer approves or edits the plan. 2. Claude implements in small steps, running tests and the linter itself; the secrets hook blocks any commit with credentials. 3. Engineer reviews the diff locally and annotates anything non-obvious. 4. Pull request opened, kept under an agreed size; the CI review bot (lesson 7.2) adds comments. 5. A human reviewer decides; the author answers review questions themselves. 2. Verification checklist Dimension Check Correctness New behaviour has tests, including at least one failure or edge case, and all tests pass Security No secrets (hook passes); new inputs validated; new calls use existing scoped credentials Maintainability Follows the service's conventions; no new dependency or abstraction without a reason in the description Understanding The description explains in the author's words what changed and why, and how it behaves on an input the tests do not cover; the reviewer may ask the author to walk through any generated section 3. Measures. Median pull request cycle time and review time per pull request; pull request size distribution; incidents and reverts traced to AI-assisted changes. - People approve the plan and the merge. - Claude runs tests before a person reviews. - The understanding check requires the author's own explanation. - My measures cover speed and quality.

docs.h: How to read a CCAR-P question
docs.x: Most items give a scenario, often with an artifact (an architecture, a prompt, a trace, an evaluation result, a decision record), and ask which constraint decides it and what trade-off follows. Six habits pick the right answer: 1. Find the binding constraint. A legal obligation, a latency limit, an audit need or a budget outranks a preference, and usually rules out two options. 2. Facts come from the system that owns them. Balances and status are fetched with a tool; numbers are computed in code. Claude does the language work. 3. Enforce outside the model. Permissions, limits, idempotency and approvals live in code and gates, never only in the prompt. 4. Start simple; change on evidence. The simplest pattern, model and prompt that meet the bar, changed only when an evaluation shows a gap. 5. Measure the right thing. The slowest requests under load, cost per successful outcome, results per slice, several trials per case. 6. Find the cause before the fix. Stop at the first wrong step in the trace. A bigger model is rarely the first answer.

Remember: obligations decide the surface, reversibility decides who acts, and the simplest design that works wins. If the question says Pick Not Who should own each step? Claude for language; systems for facts; a person for irreversible or accountable steps 1.1 Everything to Claude, or everything to people The answer includes totals or prices Compute them in code 1.1 Asking Claude to calculate Which component fails first? Apply the stated load or trust condition to each step in order 1.2 Fixing the weakest part in general A procedure reused by many teams, with one owner A Skills-based pattern 1.3 Copying the prompt into each app Several independent sub-tasks Parallel subagents, trace IDs, checkpoints, coverage check 1.4 Multi-agent for dependent steps Proposals under a cost ceiling The biggest gain on the stated goal within the ceiling 1.5 The fastest option over budget Data must stay in the firm's cloud That cloud's surface; accept feature lag and owning the loop 1.6 Zero data retention (it is not residency) Hours-long agent, small team, no residency rule Claude Managed Agents 1.6 Building a loop and sandbox HIPAA BAA or zero data retention required Self-hosted loop on a covered surface 1.6 Managed Agents (not eligible) Pattern Pick it when Watch out for Augmented LLM (one call with tools or retrieval) One bounded task, tight latency A tool does not make it an agent Workflow (chain, route, parallel, evaluator-optimizer) Steps can be listed in advance Cost and latency add up per step Agent (the model chooses the steps) The path differs every time Bound it: budgets, permissions, approvals Skills-based Governed procedures reused across many tasks Review third-party Skills before use {wide}

Remember: the smallest tier that meets every constraint, a plain prompt, stable content first, and memory for what must last. If the question says Pick Not Which model tier? Smallest that passes every binding constraint, per route 2.1 The top tier everywhere "to be safe" Output inconsistent Fix the missing scope, format or edge rule 2.2 A rigid template that kills legitimate variation Code parses the reply Structured outputs with a JSON schema 2.3 "Reply in JSON" in the prompt Errors in multi-step reasoning Native thinking for that task 2.3 Thinking on every simple call Where can tokens be cut? Stale tool output, duplicates, unused fields; keep task facts 2.4 Cutting the passage that holds the answer Cache hit rate fell Move dynamic content after the breakpoint 2.5 A timestamp at the top Long agent repeats work or forgets decisions Memory tool for progress; context editing for stale results 2.6 A bigger window, or restarting without notes Where to spend reasoning effort Planning and hard steps, not routine calls 2.6 Maximum effort everywhere - Out of room: too big to send (rejected) or the reply hits its limit (cut off). Count tokens, reserve output room. Caching is not memory. 2.4 2.5

Remember: least privilege, the binding constraint first, and no retry without an idempotency key. If the question says Pick Not A customer might see another's orders Authorization at the data, per tenant 3.2 "Tell the model to verify the user" Secrets in the system prompt Secret store; tools use credentials server-side 3.2 "Users never see the prompt" The agent has tools no task uses Remove or scope them; tool search for large sets 3.1 Better descriptions for 140 tools Latency binds, accuracy has margin Fewer retrieved passages, caching 3.3 A larger tier (slower) A failure went unnoticed for weeks The signal that shows it: traces, stop reasons, quality sampling 3.4 More error alerts Small, stable corpus Full-corpus context with caching 3.5 Building a RAG pipeline Product codes or IDs in questions Hybrid search; filter by scope first 3.5 Embeddings alone One app, tight latency / several Claude clients Direct API / an MCP server 3.6 Agent-to-agent for a lookup Duplicates after client timeouts Idempotency key from the business action 3.8 Fewer retries, a prompt instruction 429 bursts when a batch job runs Backoff with jitter; separate workspace limits 3.8 Immediate retries Primary model overloaded for 20 minutes Bounded retries, then a tested fallback 3.8 Retrying forever Data shape Retrieval method Unstructured text Chunked index: dense, sparse or hybrid Structured records Query or API with filters, not embeddings Live state A tool call to the owning system Codebases Agentic search: list, grep, open

Remember: derive the test from the business decision, read it by slice and by trial, and treat the judge as an instrument. If the question says Pick Not A failure passed the suite The missing dimension or grading target 4.1 A higher threshold on a measured metric What should the evaluation measure? The business outcome, on the deployed distribution 4.2 A convenient proxy, typical cases only Judge prefers first or longer answers Swap order; rubric with no credit for length 4.3 Raising the judge's temperature Judge scores its own model higher, or drifts A different judge model; pin and recalibrate 4.3 Dropping the human comparison A comparison reversed when rerun Several trials per case, paired by case 4.4 More cases, one run each Find the root cause First wrong step in the trace 4.5 Switching models Spend concentrated in one route Fix that route; check the cache hit rate 4.6 Cutting quality controls Snapshot retires; one category below floor Re-tune, re-run, switch before retirement 4.7 Lowering the floor; deferring past retirement Judge bias Correction Position Swap order, keep consistent verdicts Verbosity Criteria that give no credit for length Self-preference Judge from a different model Drift Pin the judge; recalibrate on human labels

Remember: assume the model can be fooled; the controls must still hold. If the question says Pick Not Injected text in a document, tool result or MCP response Treat it as data; authorize actions in code 5.2 A prompt rule; a chat-input classifier A third-party Skill or MCP server Approved source, review, pin, sandbox without secrets 5.2 Trusting it once it is listed Social engineering for another's data Scope data access to the session's identity 5.1 Refusing the legitimate use The safety check is unavailable Fail closed for money, data or safety 5.1 Fail open to stay available Which risk is highest? Anonymous access, shared capacity, critical dependencies 5.3 Risks already removed by design Where should a person approve? Before irreversible or costly steps; pause only that run 5.4 Gating every step; review after the fact Residency or retention obligation Surface and region for where; retention settings for how long 5.5 One control for both Different results across groups Fix the source: data, framing or evaluation 5.6 Removing the attribute but not its proxies

Remember: promise only what you can measure, and hand over the why as well as the what. If the question says Pick Not "100% accurate" or "never wrong" An accuracy floor on an evaluation set, plus review 6.1 Accepting it with a disclaimer Defining an SLA Percentile, window, load, breach rule, response 6.1 An average, or every request A decision record misses a constraint State the trade-off, rejected options, residual risk with evidence 6.2 Claiming certainty about model behaviour Handoff blocks the receiving team The missing assumption, dependency or runbook 6.3 A diagram alone

Remember: package once, enforce centrally, pre-approve unattended runs, and keep a person accountable. If the question says Pick Not A workflow proven on one team A plugin in an org marketplace, required via managed settings 7.1 Copying folders; per-team forks No one may use risky modes Managed settings disable bypassPermissions and auto 7.1 A line in CLAUDE.md A CI run must never wait for input dontAsk with allow and deny rules, plus hooks 7.2 bypassPermissions Never read secrets or push to main Deny rules (they hold in every mode) or a hook 7.2 An instruction AI-written code passes its tests The author explains it; a human approves 7.3 Merging because tests pass

- 70 items in 120 minutes is about 1 minute 40 seconds each. Ten items are unscored and not marked, so treat every item as scored. Read how many responses to select before the options. - Every "Not" above is a real trap. If an option sounds safe but does not touch the cause, it is probably wrong. - The score is scaled to 1,000 with 720 to pass, so a raw percentage does not convert directly. Aim for 80% or more in the practice tests.

An online home-goods retailer whose support centre handles 95,000 contacts a month, most of them repeat questions that depend on live order data.

Hollis & Grant Home, based in Columbus, Ohio, sells furniture and homewares online in North America, about 2.1 million orders a year. Its support centre handles 95,000 contacts a month : 55% by chat and 45% by email. Volume rises to 2.5 times normal in November and December.

Contact type Share Where the answer lives Order status ("where is my order?") 38% Order Management System, live Returns and refunds 24% Returns portal and refund policy Product questions (assembly, care, dimensions) 21% Product manuals and help centre Account and billing 9% CRM and payment provider Complaints 8% Needs a person

- Average handling time: 7.5 minutes per chat, 11 minutes per email. - Customer satisfaction (CSAT): 78% . First-contact resolution: 64% . - 120 support agents at a loaded cost of $32 an hour . - Refunds over $250 need a supervisor's approval.

System Role Notes Order Management System Live order and delivery status API, 95th-percentile response 250 ms Returns portal Creates returns and refunds API; refund rules are configured here Product catalogue 8,000 products, 2,300 PDF manuals Manuals change when a product is revised Help centre 400 articles Updated weekly by the support content team CRM Customer history and contact records Agents work every contact here

- Chat: first response within 3 seconds at the 95th percentile. Email: reply within 4 hours . - Card numbers are handled by a PCI-certified payment provider and must never enter the model's context. - The approved run budget for AI is $18,000 a month , including peak season. - Implementation is estimated at $250,000 one-off, plus $6,000 a month for hosting, monitoring and support.

- System prompt, policies and tool definitions: a stable 6,000 tokens . - A typical chat runs 4 turns . Each turn adds about 2,500 tokens of conversation and retrieved or tool content, and produces about 300 tokens of output.

Stakeholder Cares most about Director of Customer Experience (sponsor) CSAT, resolution, peak-season coverage Head of E-commerce Engineering Integration effort, reliability, on-call load Finance business partner Run cost, payback, headcount assumptions Support team leads Escalation quality, agent workload
A US teaching hospital where physicians spend too long writing discharge summaries, summaries are often incomplete, and every word is protected health information.

Lakeview Regional Medical Center is a 640-bed teaching hospital in Minneapolis, Minnesota, with about 2,900 discharges a month . Every discharge needs a discharge summary: the hospital course, diagnoses, procedures, medications at discharge, results still pending, and follow-up instructions for the patient and their primary care doctor.

- Physicians spend about 2.1 hours a day on documentation; a discharge summary takes 35 minutes on average. - The coding team returns 12% of summaries for missing or unclear information, which delays billing by an average of 4 days . - 1 in 7 discharges is delayed past noon because the summary is not signed.

docs.h: How a discharge summary is written today
docs.x: 1. The physician reads the stay's notes in the electronic health record (EHR): admission note, daily progress notes, consult notes, procedure reports. 2. They write the hospital course and list diagnoses and procedures. 3. They copy the discharge medication list from the pharmacist's medication reconciliation. 4. They check for results that are still pending. 5. They write follow-up instructions and book follow-up appointments. 6. They sign the summary, which is sent to the patient's primary care doctor. 7. Coders assign diagnosis and procedure codes from the signed summary.

System Role Notes EHR Clinical record FHIR API for notes, results, medications Pharmacy system Medication reconciliation The authoritative discharge medication list Scheduling system Follow-up appointments API Coding system Diagnosis and procedure codes Used by certified coders Hospital SSO Staff identity and roles Every action must be attributable to a person

- Everything in a summary is protected health information under HIPAA . Any vendor that processes it needs a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). - The hospital's cloud is AWS, with a BAA in place; data must stay in the United States . - Clinical documents and their audit trail are kept for 6 years . - A physician must review and sign every summary ; nothing is sent unsigned. The system must not suggest medication changes.
- The notes for a typical stay come to about 30,000 tokens ; long stays reach 140,000 tokens (95th percentile). - A finished summary is about 1,500 tokens .

Stakeholder Cares most about Chief Medical Information Officer (sponsor) Physician time, summary quality Chief Nursing Officer Discharge timing, patient instructions Privacy and compliance officer HIPAA, BAA, audit trail Physician representatives Accuracy, not adding review burden Health IT director EHR integration, support
A B2B software company rolling out Claude Code to 420 engineers, and using it for a large codebase-wide migration with a hard deadline.

Northgate Software, based in Seattle, Washington, builds a B2B finance platform. It has 420 engineers in 38 teams , working on 160 services written in Java, TypeScript and Python, spread across a main monorepo and about 40 smaller repositories. It is SOC 2 certified and sells to banks, so its customers audit its controls.

1. Roll out Claude Code to every engineer in a controlled way: shared settings, approved tools and Skills, and a spending limit. 2. Migrate off a deprecated logging library. A security advisory requires every service to move to the new library. Before teams start, the platform team needs an audit of all 160 services within two weeks : whether each service uses the old library, where, in what patterns, and how risky the change is. 3. Speed up incident diagnosis. On-call engineers spend about 30% of incident time searching logs and dashboards. 4. Add an assistant to the product. The product team plans a Claude-powered assistant inside the finance platform for Northgate's 60 bank customers (tenants). The largest tenant has 4,000 users; the smallest has 40. Each bank must only ever see its own data, and Northgate bills AI usage back to each bank.

- Pull request cycle time: median 26 hours from opening to merge. - Last year: 2 security incidents caused by secrets committed to repositories. - A manual audit of one service for the logging migration takes an engineer about 2.5 hours .

System Role Notes Source control Monorepo plus ~40 repositories Branch protection; two approvals to merge CI pipeline Builds, tests, security scans Runs on every pull request Observability stack Logs, metrics, traces Read access for engineers; on-call has more Internal developer portal Service catalogue and owners Lists all 160 services and their teams

- Source code may only be sent to vendors approved under the SOC 2 vendor process. - Production write access is restricted to on-call engineers and goes through change management. - AI tooling budget: $40 per engineer per month on average. - Secrets must never be read into an AI tool's context or written to logs.

Stakeholder Cares most about VP Engineering (sponsor) Delivery speed, consistent adoption across teams Platform team lead Shared configuration, the migration audit, support load Security lead Secrets, permissions, SOC 2 evidence Team champions (one per team) Practical workflows, training their teams
A property and auto insurer whose claims intake team keys every new claim by hand, misses its acknowledgement SLA and makes costly keying errors.

Prairie State Mutual, based in Des Moines, Iowa, is a mid-sized property and auto insurer with customers in the United States and the European Union. It receives about 18,000 new claims a month (first notice of loss).

Channel Share What arrives Email 60% A free-text description, often with photos and attachments Web form 30% Structured fields plus uploaded photos and documents Scanned mail 10% Handwritten or printed forms, sometimes with medical reports Fourteen intake handlers read each claim, key 31 fields into ClaimsCore (the claims system of record), check that the policy was active on the date of loss, request any missing documents, and send an acknowledgement to the customer. Measured baseline (last quarter's operations data): - Average handling time: 22 minutes per claim . - Keying errors: 6% of claims have at least one wrong field (from a monthly quality sample of 400 claims). Each error takes 35 minutes of rework later. - Acknowledgement SLA (within one business day): met 81% of the time. Target: 98% . - Loaded handler cost: $48 an hour .

docs.h: What Prairie State is considering next
docs.x: - Fast-track for small auto glass claims. About 2,400 windshield claims a month , averaging $420 , almost never disputed. Claims operations wants them paid within a day when the policy covers glass, instead of the current five days. - Claim prioritization. A queue score so that the most urgent claims (injuries, uninhabitable homes) reach adjusters first.

System Role Notes ClaimsCore System of record for claims REST API for creating and updating claims Policy Admin Policy status, cover and limits API, 95th-percentile response 300 ms Fraud rules engine Scores each claim against fixed rules Owned by the Special Investigations team Document store Holds every attachment Retains documents for 7 years

- Claims contain personal data; injury claims also contain health information from medical reports. - EU claimants are covered by GDPR ; their data must be processed in the EU. US customers' data stays in the US. - The regulator does not allow automated claim denials : a licensed adjuster makes every denial decision. Payouts over $10,000 need a senior adjuster's approval.

- A typical claim package is about 9,000 tokens ; the 95th percentile is 40,000 tokens (long medical reports). 95% of packages are under 20 pages; the longest run to about 120 pages. - The extraction instructions and the 31-field schema add a stable 4,000 tokens to every request. - A drafted acknowledgement is about 1,200 tokens of output including the extracted fields.

Stakeholder Cares most about VP Claims Operations (sponsor) The SLA and handling time Head of Compliance Regulator rules, audit evidence, GDPR Claims IT lead ClaimsCore integration, support load Intake team lead Workload, quality, how the team's role changes
A system in which a model uses tools in a loop to reach a goal, choosing its own next steps instead of following a fixed path set in code. Also: agents, AI agent
The cycle an agent runs: Claude replies, the code runs any tools it asked for, the results go back, and this repeats until Claude ends its turn or a limit is reached. Also: agent loop
AWS's managed service for foundation models, through which Claude can be used inside an AWS account. Also: Bedrock
A record of who did what and when, including an agent's actions and tool calls, kept for review, compliance and investigating incidents. Also: audit logs, audit trail
A systematic skew in output, such as favoring certain groups, viewpoints or answer positions. Found by testing varied inputs and reviewing the results. Also: biased
Splitting documents into smaller passages for indexing and retrieval. Chunk size and where the boundaries fall decide what retrieval can find. Also: chunk, chunks
A safeguard that stops calling a failing tool or service after repeated errors, so the system fails fast instead of piling up retries. Also: circuit breakers
References from Claude's answer to the exact source passages behind it, so a reader can check each claim. Also: citation, cite sources
Anthropic's library, for Python and TypeScript, for building agents on the same agent loop, tools and context management that power Claude Code. Also: Agent SDK
Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads code, edits files and runs commands, in the terminal, an IDE, the desktop app or the browser.
Anthropic's hosted service that runs agents in a managed sandbox, with sessions and events, so you do not have to build and operate the agent loop yourself. Also: Managed Agents
A Markdown file that Claude Code loads at the start of a session, holding instructions such as build commands and coding conventions. It can be set for the user, the project or a single directory.
A tool that lets Claude run code in a sandbox to analyze data, do calculations and create files. Also: code execution
Summarizing the earlier part of a long conversation to free space in the context window while keeping the facts still needed. Also: compact, auto-compact
How well a stated confidence matches real accuracy. Well-calibrated scores can be used to send low-confidence cases to a person. Also: calibration, calibrated, well-calibrated

The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can consider in one request: the system prompt, the conversation so far, tool definitions and results, and its own reply. Whatever does not fit is not seen. Also: context length
An Anthropic technique that adds a short explanation of where each chunk fits in its document before the chunk is embedded and keyword-indexed, which cuts the number of failed retrievals.
A request setting that tells the model how much reasoning and how many tokens to spend, trading answer quality against speed and cost.
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text, so texts with similar meaning have nearby embeddings. Used for semantic search. Also: embeddings
Routing a case from the automated system to a person, triggered by rules such as low confidence, high value, a policy exception or the customer asking for one. Also: escalate, escalated, escalates

A repeatable test of a model, prompt or agent against a set of cases with expected outcomes, scored by code, by people or by a model. Used to compare versions and catch regressions. Also: eval, evals, evaluation, evaluations
Waiting longer after each failed attempt before retrying, usually with some random jitter, so retries do not overload the service. Also: backoff, retry with backoff

A mode in which Claude reasons step by step in thinking blocks before giving its final answer, within a token budget. It helps on complex, multi-step problems at the cost of extra tokens and time. Also: thinking budget, thinking blocks

Putting a few worked examples of input and desired output in the prompt so the model follows their format and judgment. The examples should vary, or the model copies their surface details. Also: few-shot, multishot, few-shot examples
A second working directory on its own branch of the same repository, so several Claude Code sessions can work in parallel without touching each other's files. Also: worktree, worktrees
A curated set of test cases with known correct answers that evaluations are scored against. Also: golden set, gold set, ground truth
Telling Claude to base its answer only on material you supply, and to say plainly when that material does not cover the question. Also: grounded
A check outside the model's own judgment that blocks or corrects unsafe or invalid actions, such as input validation, an allow list or a hook. Also: guardrails

A confident statement that is not supported by the source material or by fact. Reduced by grounding answers in supplied documents, asking for quotes or citations, and allowing the answer "I don't know". Also: hallucinate, hallucinated
Passing a task, together with the context needed to continue it, from one agent to another or from an agent to a person. Also: handoffs, hand off
Running Claude Code without the interactive session, using the -p flag, for scripts and CI pipelines. Output can be plain text or JSON.

A command that runs automatically at a set point in an agent's lifecycle, for example before a tool call (PreToolUse) or after it (PostToolUse). Unlike an instruction in a prompt, a hook always runs. Also: hooks, PreToolUse, PostToolUse

A design in which a person reviews or approves certain actions or outputs before they take effect, usually the high-impact or low-confidence ones. Also: human-in-the-loop, HITL, human review, human approval
Combining keyword search, such as BM25, with embedding search, so both exact terms like product codes and differently worded passages are found. Also: BM25

The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. An idempotency key lets an agent retry a write, such as a payment, without making it twice. Also: idempotent, idempotency key, idempotency keys
Improving a prompt or an output over several rounds, changing one thing at a time and checking the effect of each change. Also: iterate, iterating, iterative
The time between sending a request and getting the response. For chat, the time to the first token matters most. Also: time to first token, TTFT
Giving an agent or tool only the permissions its task needs, which limits the damage a mistake or an attack can do. Also: least-privilege

Using a model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric. Its grades need checking against human ones, because judges have biases such as preferring longer answers or the first answer shown. Also: LLM-as-judge, LLM judge, LLM-as-a-judge, model-graded
A Messages API feature that connects a request to remote MCP servers directly, without running your own MCP client.
A program that offers tools, resources or prompts over MCP, for example in front of a database, a file system or a business application. Also: MCP servers
A tool that lets Claude save and read information in files outside its context window, so knowledge can carry over between sessions.

An API for submitting large groups of requests that are processed asynchronously, usually within 24 hours, at half the normal price. Suited to work that does not need an answer straight away. Also: Batch API, batch processing, Message Batches
The main Claude API: you send a conversation as a list of user and assistant messages, plus optional system prompt and tools, and receive the next assistant message.

Restricting retrieval to documents whose metadata, such as date, product, region or access rights, matches the request, before or alongside similarity search. Also: metadata filters, metadata filtering
Microsoft's Azure AI platform, through which Claude models are also available. Also: Azure AI Foundry
An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server offers tools, resources and prompts; an MCP client inside the application connects to it. Also: MCP
Moving an application to a newer model: rerunning evaluations, adjusting prompts and settings, and rolling the change out gradually. Also: migrating to a new model, model upgrade
Claude comes in tiers: Haiku for fast, low-cost, high-volume work, Sonnet as a balanced default, and Opus for the hardest reasoning. Choosing per task balances quality, speed and cost.
Several agents, usually an orchestrator and specialized subagents, working on one task. It gains parallel work and separate contexts at the cost of more tokens and coordination. Also: multi-agent
Being able to see what a system is doing from its traces, logs and metrics, such as each model call, tool call, delay and cost in an agent run. Also: tracing, traces
The agent or code that splits a task, hands the parts to workers or subagents and combines what they return. Also: coordinator, lead agent, orchestrator-workers
The Claude Code setting for how much Claude may do without asking, from asking before every edit or command to accepting edits automatically. Plan mode is one of the modes. Also: permission modes

Information that can identify a person, such as a name, address, ID number or health record. Often removed or masked before text reaches a model or a log. Also: personally identifiable information, personal data
A package that bundles Claude Code extensions, such as skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers, so a team can install them together. Also: plugins
A catalog, usually a repository with a marketplace file, from which users find and install plugins. Also: marketplace
A judge's tendency to prefer an answer because of where it appears, first or second. Countered by running the comparison in both orders.
Precision is the share of flagged items that really are positive; recall is the share of real positives that were flagged. Raising one usually lowers the other.

Reusing the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix, such as long instructions or a reference document, across requests. Cached reads cost much less and return faster, but only an exact match of the prefix up to the cache breakpoint is reused. Also: cache breakpoint, cache_control

An attack in which instructions hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page, email, document or tool result, try to make it act against its user or developer. Also: indirect prompt injection, injection
A reusable prompt with fixed instructions and placeholders for the parts that change, so a team gets consistent results from the same kind of request. Also: prompt templates, template, templates
A cap on requests or tokens per minute for an organization. Going over it returns HTTP 429, which a client should handle by waiting and retrying with backoff. Also: rate limits, HTTP 429, 429
Running an evaluation suite again after a change, such as a new prompt, model or tool, to confirm that what worked before still works. Also: regression test, regression tests, regression suite
A second pass that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance, usually with a stronger model, so only the best few go into the prompt. Also: reranker, rerank
Fetching relevant passages from a knowledge source when a question arrives and placing them in the prompt, so the answer is grounded in that content rather than in the model's memory. Also: RAG
Running commands in an isolated environment with limits on file system and network access, so an agent can act with fewer approval prompts at lower risk. Also: sandbox, sandboxed

Information whose exposure could harm people or the organization, such as personal, financial, health or client-confidential data. It belongs only in approved tools, and only as much as the task needs. Also: confidential data, confidential information, sensitive information

A folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions, plus optional scripts and resources, that Claude loads only when a task needs it. Skills work in Claude Code, the API and claude.ai. Also: skills, Agent Skills, SKILL.md
A command typed as /name in Claude Code. Built-in commands control the session; custom ones run saved prompts. Also: slash commands, custom command, custom commands

The field in an API response that says why generation ended, for example end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence or tool_use. An agent loop reads it to decide whether to run a tool or finish. Also: stop_reason, end_turn
Receiving a response in pieces, as server-sent events, while it is being generated, so users see output at once instead of waiting for the whole message.
Constraining a response to a given JSON schema so code can parse it reliably. A tool with an input schema can be used the same way. Also: structured output
An agent started by another agent to handle one subtask in its own context window. It returns only its result, which keeps the parent's context small. Also: subagents, sub-agent
Instructions sent separately from the conversation that set Claude's role, rules and background for every turn of it. Also: system prompts
A sampling setting that controls randomness: lower values give more predictable wording, higher values more varied wording. It does not make answers more accurate.
The unit models read and write text in, on average a little less than one English word. Context windows, rate limits and prices are all counted in tokens. Also: tokens

The text in a tool definition that says what the tool does, when to use it and what its inputs mean. Claude picks tools mainly from these descriptions, so vague or overlapping ones cause wrong choices. Also: tool descriptions
The message that returns a tool's output to Claude, matched to the request by its ID. Marking it as an error lets Claude see that the call failed and recover. Also: tool_result, is_error

Letting Claude call functions you define. Claude returns a tool_use request with arguments, your code runs the tool, and you send the output back as a tool result. Also: function calling, tool call, tool calls, tool calling
A store that indexes embeddings and returns those nearest to a query's embedding. Also: vector store, vector index

Checking AI output against a trusted reference before it is used, such as the source documents, known data or an expert, with more checking where the stakes are higher. Also: verify, verified, fact-check, fact-checking
Google Cloud's AI platform, through which Claude can be used inside a Google Cloud project. Also: Google Vertex AI, Google Cloud Vertex AI
Tags such as document or instructions, written in angle brackets, used to separate the parts of a prompt so Claude can tell instructions, data and examples apart.

An arrangement for eligible organizations under which prompts and outputs are not stored after the response is returned, apart from what the law or the arrangement requires. Also: ZDR, zero data retention
